# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: The flow runs in a sensible order: market, then context and window, then the problem's size, then what else is hard and how they cope today, then who asks and who gets the link.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), so the context felt asked twice around the window screen.
founder.missing: The belief questions (8 and 9) only ask about a job failing on a wrong request; nothing asks about the other half of my problem, how many researchers over-request and leave reserved GPUs idle (the two-to-three-times padding), which is where most of the 30% to 59% waste comes from.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 4 asks what I'd most like made easier before screen 5 walks me through how my last job's guessing actually went, so I'm choosing a fix before recalling the event (and screens 1 and 2 both say '1 of 4', which is confusing).
PRIMARY.missing: What a failed job cost me: how far into the run it got killed and how many hours or days of work and GPU time I lost. Also whether I pad my requests to be safe and what that over-requesting costs in queue time, and how I estimate today (past sacct/seff numbers, short test runs, copying a colleague's script).

screens.why2: Partition, queue, GPU-hour allocation and getting software working on the cluster are everyday words on a SLURM or K8s cluster, so a researcher reads every row first time.
screens.why3: Every row is something a researcher does themselves around submitting a job on a shared cluster.
screens.why4: The rivals are distinct and in our words, but the own row only restates the circumstance as a three-item list, and 'Moving data on and off the cluster' sits partly outside the submit moment.
screens.why5: The rows and the test sentence still say what I typed and leak nothing of Expanse.
screens.why7: The own row is first, there are four rivals and the belief can go either way, but the own row is the circumstance said again rather than the part that goes wrong (the job failing or the GPUs sitting idle), and no Check note flags it, so the belief nearly reads as a tautology.
screens.instead: Own row: 'Sizing a job so it neither fails nor wastes GPUs', with the same four rivals (partition or queue, data on and off, software working, checking the allocation).

screens.why1: Right after the problem's importance, it is natural to ask how my researchers handle sizing today and how it goes, before Keel drafts the stranger's scale.
screens.why2: 'Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster' is how I talk about the problem, and the hint's 'the one step that hurts' points me straight to guessing the request at submit.
screens.why3: I know exactly what researchers do at submit (guess, then pad two to three times) and how it turns out, because that is the waste we measured on the 122k-job cluster.
screens.why4: The only chip is 'I'm not sure', the right escape for a founder's two boxes, and both boxes take my answer whole within their word limits.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my job and actor words and adds nothing of Expanse's product to the question.
screens.why7: My two boxes give the act and its means (guessing and padding two to three times) and three rungs on one measure, reserved against used; the first rung is a working one ('Ran first time, sized about right') and the rest grade padding worse, so Keel can add the failed and never-ran rungs below and the belief can go either way.

screens.why1: Right after I said how researchers size jobs today, I'm checking the five ways that last submission could have gone, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Ran first time, holding twice what it used, failed partway and resubmitted: these are exactly how people on a SLURM cluster talk about a job.
screens.why3: Any researcher knows whether their last job ran, died mid-run, or sat on GPUs it never touched; sacct and seff show them that much.
screens.why4: The five cover the real cases, but 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' and 'Never ran to the end' blur, since a job that failed partway also never ran to the end that time.
screens.why5: The rows are mine, but the line Keel set under 'holding about twice' counts 2x over-requesting as working, and 2x to 3x padding is the very waste I'm selling against.
screens.why7: There is a working first rung and a clean outright failure last, but rungs 2 and 3 grade idle reservation while rungs 4 and 5 grade whether the job finished (the card's own example of a mixed measure), and the default line counts 2x waste against the belief.
screens.instead: Same five rows, line moved under 'Ran first time, sized about right', and the last rung reworded to 'Killed and never resubmitted' so it doesn't overlap 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted'.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is a natural last setup step before the study goes out to researchers, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain, but the picked option "Lock and record the face Keel preselects" needs a second read: does it mean I keep Keel's default interviewer, or that I record something myself?
screens.why3: As the founder I know who my researchers are and can judge whether an AI video interviewer suits them, so I can answer this.
screens.why4: Accepting Keel's preselected face is a fair option, but 'lock and record' is awkward, and I can't tell from it how it differs from simply picking a face.
screens.why5: The screen is about delivery only; it neither changes my study's words nor leaks the product or roles to respondents.
screens.instead: Who should ask them your questions? -- Keel's AI interviewer (keep the face Keel picked) / Choose a different AI face / Record the questions in my own voice and face

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, picking how researchers answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: The three options are plain, and each says exactly what the researcher would do (talk, type or tap).
screens.why3: I know my researchers. They sit at a terminal and would rather read and tap than talk to a video, so I can answer this straight from what I know.
screens.why4: AI voice, text, or the respondent's choice covers the field with no overlap; the descriptions are clear and no escape is needed for a format choice.
screens.why5: It keeps my segment's words ('researchers and ML engineers'), and nothing of Expanse's product leaks to a respondent here.

screens.why1: After choosing how researchers answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending the study out.
screens.why2: Three plain ways to reach people that I read at once: people I know, a Keel search list, or one open link posted where the researchers already are.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach: researchers I have met on HPC sites and labs, plus the cluster communities where an open link would land.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the real cases, but the second option's 'Contacts page' points at a Keel screen I have not seen in this flow, so it needs a second read.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or my roles leaks; it is purely about distribution, and my pick of people I know by name is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (each gets their own link) / A list I build with Keel's contact search (a link for each, I send them) / A group, with one open link I post where they already are (each signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title with the number that decides it, Frequency at 4 counted, and the card adds that 5 were needed, so I know why the stage did not call.
screens.why_b2: The tally and the cards show what was counted and where each bar sits (6 of 7 at the bar, 4 counted against 5 needed), but the kicker '4 TO 7 COUNTED' and the gap between 7 answering and 4 counted take a second look, because the page never says why three people dropped out.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are recognisably mine, but Prevalence and Frequency are put as 'had a job fail on a wrong request'; my belief is that everyone has to guess sizes at every submission and pads by two to three times, not that 8 in 10 had a job die this week or on 3 to 5 days out of 5.
screens.why_b4: Apart from '5 needed to call it' on each card, which only implies I need more counted answers, the page says nothing about what this means for Expanse or what to do next; 'What it measures' is a generic method line.
screens.why_b5: Prevalence is called 'Holding up' at exactly the bar with only 7 people, and the low n is not flagged there; my own launch figures (59%, 30% to 40%) also sit under the title where they could read as findings from this study.
screens.instead: Too few to call: Frequency, Importance and Current solution each had 4 counted where 5 are needed (3 of 7 skipped the week or guessed), so get at least one more researcher who submitted jobs this week; Prevalence (6 of 7 guess sizes at submit) holds, but only just and on 7 people.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I know it held and by exactly what count.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against out of 7, with my bar marked at 6 (at least 8 in 10), so what is counted, over how many, and where the bar is are all plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The 'at least 8 in 10' band is mine and the event is recognisably my under-request failure, but the segment drops 'on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs'; the 'Asked' line also carries a stray '— the most recent time it happened' tag that a yes/no gate never asked.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7, at your bar exactly' plus a pointer to the next two cards is a navigation line; it does not say that one more No would sink the belief, or what that means for leading with failures rather than waste.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is said outright, and holding exactly at the bar is called 'Holding up', not strong.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 7 researchers on 100+ GPU SLURM/K8s clusters had a job fail on a wrong request this week, exactly your 8-in-10 bar, so one more No would drop it; treat it as a lean and check Frequency and Importance before leading your pitch with failed jobs.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits at the top with '4 counted · 5 needed to call it' right under it, so I know the call and the number behind it at once.
screens.why_b2: Median 4 on a working-days axis is plain, but the axis starts at 0 when nobody could answer 0, and 'your bar · 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)' mixes the 5 I need with the 2-in-3 bar, so I had to read it twice to see where the bar sits.
screens.why_b3: 'Have a job fail on a wrong request' is recognisably my problem, but it reads as failures only; my belief is the guess at submit time, which mostly shows up as over-requesting and idle GPUs, and that half is gone.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't say that all 4 counted are inside my range, so one more counted answer would likely settle it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted, why two were left out) and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than the answers carry.
screens.instead: All 4 counted are inside your 3 to 5 days (middle answer 4), but 5 are needed to call it: get one more researcher to answer and this likely holds.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both, so I know where it stands and why.
screens.why_b2: The caption says it plainly: 4 people, each picked two, bars count picks (8). My row is marked and leads with 3, and the strip shows 3 for, 1 against and 1 empty cell, with the marker at 4 of 5.
screens.why_b3: The rivals are the rows I checked, but my own row comes back as 'Guessing memory, GPUs and run time' rather than my 'Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs'; that is just my circumstance said again, so I recognise it but it is not my wording.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me I need one more counted researcher, that a 'for' would hold it at 4 of 5, or that one 'against' sinks it at 3 of 5.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout, the two uncounted people are named with their reasons, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps 3 of 4 from being oversold (Mei-Ling's 'would rather not say' is only printed twice, which is untidy but not misleading).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted with 5 needed.
screens.why_b2: The chart's counts and my line under 'Ran, holding about twice what it used' read at once, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with the marker at 4 takes a second look: is the bar 4 of 5 people, or 2 in 3 of whoever is counted?
screens.why_b3: It names Current solution, my act of guessing memory, time and GPUs before submitting, my rungs word for word, and the line I placed.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't say that 3 of the 4 counted already land below my line, or that one more counted researcher is what I need.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible, names why Mei-Ling and Rafael were not counted, and calls the small group a lean, not a call, with no claim beyond the four.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 counted fell short (two held three times what they used, one failed and was resubmitted), so it leans your way; get one more researcher's last job to call it.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: Importance is my dimension, but the belief line still says 'Guessing memory, GPUs and run time' instead of the row I settled on, 'Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs'; I recognise it, but it isn't my current wording.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next: not to get more researchers through to a counted answer, and not whether the data and software pain Kwabena names should change how I pitch.
screens.why_b5: The single voice is shown as '1 against · 1 asked' and 'On their own (1)', so it is never passed off as a pattern and the low n stays visible.
screens.why_b6: Kwabena's line, that sizes from last week's runs are fine and his day goes on moving data and getting libraries to agree, gives me a rival pain I did not type and a segment that already sizes well.
screens.instead: Too few to call (4 of 5 needed); the one against sizes from past runs and loses the day to data movement and broken libraries instead, so get more researchers counted, and check whether the teams that already size from history are a segment Expanse won't win.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is obvious this checks whether I am the right person: someone who submits jobs to a big GPU cluster.
screens.why2: Cluster, GPUs and jobs are everyday words in my work, so I can answer this on first read.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our cluster is and that I run my fine-tuning jobs on it, though someone on a cluster near 100 GPUs might have to guess.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it for a gate, and the gate is right to have no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's segment is a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster, and the screen keeps only the size and drops shared, which is what makes wasting the cluster my problem.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: Do you submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with 100 or more GPUs? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a 100+ GPU cluster, asking whether a job of mine died this week is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: 'Fail on a wrong request' is clipped, so I had to read it twice to see it means my resource request; I'd say 'got killed because I asked for too little memory or time' or 'OOM'd or hit the wall time'.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether any of my jobs got killed in the last week; I look at sacct and the logs every day.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, and the two chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but 'wrong request' has drifted a little from the problem of under-requesting and getting killed mid-run, since over-requesting wastes the cluster without failing anything.
screens.why6: It is one short sentence followed by 'Yes or no', which is easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: The gate asks about the costly event, a job failing, rather than the routine of guessing a request, so someone whose jobs all finished can truly say No and the share can go either way.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did one of your jobs get killed for running out of the memory or time you asked for? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to having a job fail on a wrong request this week, asking how many days it happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I'd say a job got OOM-killed or hit its time limit because I under-requested; 'fail on a wrong request' takes a second read, since over-requesting is also 'wrong' but never kills a job.
screens.why3: I know which days my jobs died on me this week, so I can count them without guessing.
screens.why4: One button per working day from 1 to 5 covers every answer after a yes at the gate, and 'I can't recall' is the right escape.
screens.why5: It stays on jobs dying from a bad resource guess, the founder's situation, and nothing about a product or the founder's own terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'a number from 1 to 5, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold when heard.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of the window's units from 1 to the window's 5, the unit is said once, the event clause is 8 words, and the one escape 'I can't recall' is there apart, so a founder low of 2 or more can both hold and fail.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 5 working days did you have a job killed for under-requesting memory or time? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking how often a job failed on a wrong request, it makes sense to ask how that compares with the other hassles of getting a job onto the cluster.
screens.why2: Allocation, partition, queue and moving data on and off are all everyday words on a SLURM cluster; only 'your last run of jobs' is a slightly odd way to say the last time I submitted.
screens.why3: Every one of these is something I do myself around submitting a job, so I can answer from last week.
screens.why4: The guessing row is three things in one ('memory, GPUs and run time') and just repeats the situation rather than what goes wrong; 'partition or queue' is two words for one choice; and software setup and data moving sit a bit before the moment of submitting.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product leaks, but 'guessing' drifts from the real hurt, which is under-requesting and getting the job killed mid-run, toward simply naming the step everyone does.
screens.why6: One short question and five short options I can hold, with 'none of these' said last; 'GPU-hour allocation' is the only slight mouthful.
screens.why7: The own row is on the list, not first, with four rivals and 'None of these' at the first ask, so the belief can go either way; but the own row restates the circumstance and holds a list inside it, which bends A3 and the one-thing rule.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Checking the group's GPU-hour allocation · Getting software working on the cluster · Sizing a job's request so it isn't killed · Choosing which partition to submit to · Moving data on and off the cluster · None of these

screens.why1: After the screens on jobs failing from a wrong request and what I'd most like made easier, asking how sizing my last job went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Guessing memory, time and GPUs is exactly my world, but I'd say a job 'requested' twice what it used, not 'held' it, so 'holding' takes a second read.
screens.why3: I size and submit my own jobs and can check seff or sacct for what they actually used, so I know which of these happened last time.
screens.why4: There is no rung between 'about right' and 'about twice', so something like 1.5x has no home, and 'failed partway and resubmitted' sits close to 'never ran to the end' when a job died and I gave up on it.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or the founder's terms reaches me, and under-requesting killing a run mid-way, the pain I'd raise, is kept.
screens.why6: One question and five short parallel options that I can hold when heard, with the one escape said last; 'three times or more' is the longest but still says fine.
screens.why7: There is a working first rung, five rungs ordered best to worst, the shortfalls below can count for or against the belief, and 'I can't recall' fits a job I size myself; but rungs 1 to 3 grade over-reservation while 'failed partway and resubmitted' and 'never ran to the end' grade whether it ran, which is the card's own example of a rung leaving the measure.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. How did guessing its memory, time and GPUs go? Ran first time, requested about what it used · Ran first time, requested well over what it used · Hit a limit, ran after one resubmit · Hit limits, took several resubmits to finish · Never got it to run to the end; or I can't recall.
